label: Meissen Porcelain
defn: The first European hard-paste porcelain, made at the Saxon royal manufactory at Meissen from 1710 after Böttger's discovery, with enamel painting led by Höroldt and modelled figures by Kändler: Kakiemon- and chinoiserie-painted tea services, Kändler's Swan Service, Kändler's animal and commedia figures.
see: L4 Hard-Paste Porcelain;E4-17 Kakiemon;I3-5 Louis XV Style
note: Evidence: Cooper Hewitt 123 objects credited to Meissen Porcelain Manufactory; Met 186 objects by J. J. Kändler (Q73593) and 11 by J. G. Höroldt; Met culture "German, Meissen" 7. Passes §2.3 (>=50). Kändler and Höroldt are currently placed by period in artist_placements (T143, T31).

label: Sèvres Porcelain
defn: The porcelain of the French royal (later national) manufactory founded at Vincennes and moved to Sèvres in 1756, soft-paste until the 1770s and hard-paste after, famous for its ground colours, gilding and biscuit figures: bleu céleste and rose Pompadour services, biscuit figures after Falconet and Boizot, Napoleon III table services.
aliases: Vincennes-Sèvres porcelain;Manufacture nationale de Sèvres;Sèvres ware
see: L3 Soft-Paste Porcelain;L4 Hard-Paste Porcelain;I3-5 Louis XV Style
note: Evidence: Cooper Hewitt 93 objects (Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory) + 2 Vincennes; Met "French, Sèvres" 1. Passes §2.3. Vincennes (1740-1756) is a kind (phase), not a separate leaf ("Vincennes porcelain" article also exists).

label: Soft-Paste Porcelain
defn: European artificial (frit) porcelain fired at lower temperature than true porcelain, made from the Medici experiments to the French and English factories of the 18th century: Saint-Cloud and Chantilly wares, Chelsea gold-anchor figures, Worcester blue-and-white, Capodimonte figures.
see: L2 Sèvres Porcelain;L4 Hard-Paste Porcelain;E1-79 Staffordshire Pottery
note: Umbrella leaf for the manufactories that do not pass §2.3 alone; they are kinds (see kinds file). Evidence: Met classification "British / soft-paste porcelain" 51 + "French / soft-paste porcelain" 41; Cooper Hewitt Chelsea 44, Royal Worcester 33, Mennecy 14, Chantilly 9, Derby 8, Saint-Cloud 7, Longton Hall 6, Bow 4, Caughley 4, Capodimonte 3. Body-type leaf: a named manufactory leaf (Sèvres) takes precedence.

label: Hard-Paste Porcelain
defn: True (feldspathic) porcelain made in Europe after Meissen's secret spread in the 18th century, by the court and private manufactories of the German states, Austria, Italy, Scandinavia, Russia and Hungary: Du Paquier Vienna tablewares, Bustelli's Nymphenburg commedia figures, Berlin KPM view-painted vases, Doccia and Cozzi wares.
see: L1 Meissen Porcelain;L3 Soft-Paste Porcelain;E4-21 Limoges Porcelain;E4-22 Gzhel
note: Umbrella leaf for European hard-paste manufactories that do not pass alone (kinds). Defined as European: Chinese and Japanese hard-paste stays in their named-ware leaves (seam: Met also classifies Chinese export as hard-paste). Evidence: Met "German / hard-paste porcelain" 48 + "French / hard-paste porcelain" 51; Cooper Hewitt Berlin 26, Doccia 25, Fürstenberg 15, Cozzi 15, Du Paquier 13, Wallendorf 10, Imperial St Petersburg 5, Frankenthal 5; Met F. A. Bustelli (Nymphenburg) 28 objects with 2 Timeline works.

label: Medieval Stained Glass
defn: Coloured pot-metal glass painted with vitreous paint (and from c. 1300 silver stain) and leaded into windows for the churches of Latin Europe, c. 1100-1500, from Romanesque and High Gothic cathedral glazing to late Gothic workshops: Chartres and Sainte-Chapelle windows, Canterbury Miracle windows, Ebreichsdorf roundels, Strasbourg workshop of Peter Hemmel.
see: L6 Painted Glass Roundels;K4 Medieval European Architecture
note: Evidence: Met "French / glass" 455 objects (median date 1400, Medieval Art, 20 Timeline works); "Austrian / glass" 78 (Cloisters, 1390, 2 Timeline works). Also Met essay https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/stained-glass-in-medieval-europe. English Gothic glass has its own article (English Gothic stained glass windows) as a kind.

label: Painted Glass Roundels
defn: Small panes of colourless glass painted in vitreous paint and silver stain, set into domestic and cloister windows in the Low Countries, northern France and the Rhineland, c. 1480-1560, often after designs by painters: roundels from the circle of the Master of the Amsterdam Cabinet, Labours of the Months roundels, Tobias roundels.
note: Evidence: Met "South Netherlandish / glass" 75 objects (Cloisters, median 1510, 1 Timeline work). Label from the Met catalogue (Husband, The Luminous Image, 1995); no English Wikipedia article. Swiss heraldic cabinet panes are a separate below-rule item.

label: Tiffany Glass
defn: The opalescent and iridescent glass of Louis Comfort Tiffany's studios in New York (1878-1933) and the American opalescent window movement he shared with John La Farge: leaded windows, lamps, mosaics and blown Favrile vessels: Tiffany Studios wisteria lamps, Favrile vases, La Farge's Peonies Blown in the Wind window.
aliases: American opalescent glass;opalescent stained glass;Favrile glass
see: F1 Blown & Moulded Glass;I3-11 Art Nouveau
note: Evidence: Met 703 objects by L. C. Tiffany (Q312950) with 17 Timeline works; Cooper Hewitt 77 glass objects (Tiffany, Tiffany & Co., Tiffany Glass and Decorating Co.) and about 100 designs for windows (A. C. Morse 54, F. Lathrop 20, J. La Farge 17). Favrile vessels are blown glass (seam with F1). Tiffany and La Farge currently placed under Academic Art (T40) in artist_placements.

label: Limoges Enamel
defn: Enamel on copper made at Limoges, first as gilt champlevé (Œuvre de Limoges, c. 1150-1350) for reliquaries and liturgical objects, then as painted enamel and grisaille (c. 1470-1630) by dynasties of enamellers: champlevé chasses of Thomas Becket, Pénicaud triptychs, Léonard Limosin portraits, Pierre Reymond grisaille tableware.
aliases: Œuvre de Limoges;opus lemovicense;Limoges painted enamel;émail de Limoges
see: G1-43 Mosan Art;G1-36 South Staffordshire Enamels
note: Evidence: Met "French / champleve" 146 objects (median 1202, 13 Timeline works) and "French / enamels" 199 (16 Timeline works); Met L. Limosin and P. Reymond 1 Timeline work each; Cooper Hewitt 3 Limoges enamels (Martial Courteys). Limosin currently placed under Northern Renaissance painting (T24).

label: Augsburg Goldsmiths' Work
defn: The silver and gold of the guild goldsmiths of the imperial city of Augsburg, Europe's leading exporter of display plate from the late 16th to the 18th century: embossed repoussé dishes and ewers, silver-gilt toilet services, Hildesheim prince-bishop's service, enamel- and gem-mounted Baroque cabinet pieces.
note: Evidence: Met culture "German, Augsburg" 145 objects with 3 Timeline works, of which "German, Augsburg / metalwork" 50 (median 1690) plus enamels 5, horology 3; the rest is armour (Augsburg armourers, G2). Cooper Hewitt 31 goldsmiths' designs printed in Augsburg. No English Wikipedia article; Met object pages (e.g. https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/206244) use the term. Nuremberg goldsmiths (Jamnitzer) are not covered.

label: English Silver
defn: Domestic, ceremonial and church plate made by the goldsmiths of London and the English assay towns from the Tudor period to the 19th century, transformed after 1685 by Huguenot refugee silversmiths: Huguenot ewers and wine cisterns, Paul de Lamerie's Rococo tea kettles, Georgian tea services, Regency presentation plate.
see: L9 Augsburg Goldsmiths' Work;I3-5 Louis XV Style
note: Evidence: Met "British, London / metalwork" 142 objects (3 Timeline works) and "British / metalwork" 833 (8 Timeline works); Cooper Hewitt 211 silver objects made in England; Met P. de Lamerie (Q1751768) 74 objects, 1 Timeline work. Huguenot silver is a kind (school) here, attested at https://fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/plan-your-visit/exhibitions/refugee-silver-huguenots-in-britain. No English Wikipedia article "English silver". Lamerie currently placed under Louis XV Style (T162).

label: Pietra Dura
defn: Pictorial inlay of cut and fitted coloured hardstones (commesso), developed in the grand-ducal workshops of Florence from 1588 and practised in Rome, Milan, Prague and Paris: pietre dure table tops and cabinets, Cappella dei Principi panels, Badminton Cabinet.
see: I1 Carved & Inlaid Woodwork;L3 Mosaic & Tile Revetment
note: Evidence: Met "Italian / lapidary work" 95 objects (median 1630, 1 Timeline work), "Italian, Milan / lapidary work" 6 (1 Timeline), "Italian, Rome" 4, "French / lapidary work" 15. Mughal parchin kari is a related Indian tradition (see South Asia slice) and is not included here.

label: Boulle Work
defn: Marquetry of tortoiseshell and brass (with pewter and horn) cut together in première- and contre-partie sheets, perfected for Louis XIV's court by André-Charles Boulle and revived in the 19th century: Boulle commodes for the Trianon, bracket clocks and pedestals, bureaux plats.
note: Evidence: Met Timeline works by A.-C. Boulle (Q128964, 12 objects, 3 Timeline works), Pierre Gole (1) and A.-J. Oppenordt (1); Cooper Hewitt 17 Boulle prints and designs. Passes on Met Timeline. Boulle is currently placed under Baroque Painting (T27) in artist_placements. Other European marquetry (Roentgen, Oeben, Riesener) stays under the I3 style leaves where it already is.

label: Venetian Lace
defn: The needle laces of Venice, 16th-18th century, from reticella and punto in aria to the sculptural gros point and rose point that dominated European fashion before French point d'Alençon: punto in aria collars, gros point de Venise flounces, rose point cravat ends.
aliases: Point de Venise;punto Venezia;Venetian needle lace;gros point de Venise
note: Evidence: Rijksmuseum "Italian, Venice" 108 textile objects (lace flounces); Cooper Hewitt 46 needle laces made in Venice plus 20 punto in aria and about 50 reticella; Met "Italian, Venice / textiles" 518 (2 Timeline works; includes velvets). "Venetian lace" redirects to Point de Venise on English Wikipedia. Burano (19th-century revival) stays its own leaf.

label: Gobelins Tapestry
defn: Tapestry woven at the royal Gobelins Manufactory in Paris from 1662 under Le Brun, the official weaving of the French crown (The History of the King, Les Maisons royales, the Boucher Loves of the Gods).
note: admitted by owner decision (R2): below §2.3 only because the Met files European tapestry under French textiles without the manufactory

label: Beauvais Tapestry
defn: Tapestry woven at the Beauvais Manufactory from 1664, the private royal works for furniture covers and lighter subjects after Oudry and Boucher (Fêtes italiennes, Chinese Series).
note: admitted by owner decision (R2): below §2.3 only because of the data gap
